prize_parts.citation: For their formal and empirical analysis of how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic performance.

statement.case_for: Political economics supplied a unified, testable account of why policies differ across polities. It links electoral rules, constitutional design, political accountability and fiscal capacity to taxation, spending, redistribution and growth outcomes. The Persson-Tabellini programme gave the field its canonical synthesis. It also generated cross-country and later more design-based empirical tests. The Besley-Persson work on state capacity and the Besley work on political agency are a distinct, coherent second strand that makes the fiscal and institutional story complete. The work has been absorbed into public economics, macroeconomics and comparative politics, with thirty years of replication and extension, so maturity is not a concern. Common criteria favour it: conceptual originality, breadth of influence, and a long record of confirmation. In my opening I preferred a pair, Persson and Tabellini, for cleanest attribution. After reading colleagues I am moving to the trio. The proposed citation covers state capacity, and the Besley-Persson strand is not derivative of the constitutions-and-electoral-rules work.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is identification. Much of the evidence on electoral rules and constitutions rests on cross-country comparisons where adoption is endogenous. Some headline empirical findings are sensitive to specification. Credibility is weaker than in the design-based literatures I know best, such as B002 and B024. There is also thematic proximity to the 2024 institutions prize. The committee could judge this a near-term repetition, or conclude that the contribution is mainly a theoretical framework whose empirical payoff is mixed.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B027 first. He argues that it created a field with rigorous theory and credible empirical tests. He acknowledges that the electoral-rules evidence rests on cross-country identification less clean than the theory, and that a Besley third place is a judgement call.
responses.response: I agree with the qualification on identification, and I weigh it more heavily than a theorist might. I still think the prize case rests on the unifying framework and on the sharp, testable predictions it produced. Later quasi-experimental work on local electoral rules and accountability builds on those predictions. On the third name, I now side with including Besley. State capacity and political selection are a separate line that supports the proposed citation, and I no longer want to defend the narrower pair I proposed in the opening.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B027 sixth. She describes it as a coherent programme that opened a field, but says the identification of constitutional effects is weaker than in design-based literatures. She also flags overlap with Acemoglu-Johnson-Robinson and a spread of credit across the wider field.
responses.response: The identification point is fair, and it is why I do not rank B027 on design credibility alone. The work shows its distinctiveness against the 2024 prize in its focus on policy formation: electoral rules, legislative structure and the fiscal choices they produce. The 2024 prize was about long-run institutional origins of prosperity. Credit concentration is also good here. Persson and Tabellini's joint programme and the Besley-Persson state-capacity work are identifiable as a unit. Credit is less diffuse than in B015 or B024. I accept that the committee must decide whether a conceptual framework with mixed identification outweighs a sharply identified measurement advance.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B002 first. He argues that population-scale administrative data made intergenerational mobility measurable and place-specific, with credible quasi-experimental designs for neighbourhood effects. He also notes that the three-name cap forces a hard choice among Chetty, Hendren, Friedman and Katz.
responses.response: I take the measurement and policy-relevance argument seriously. This is the kind of register-data work I know well, and I rank B002 fifth, not lower. My reservations are about maturity and the strength of the exposure-effect claims, which rely on assumptions that are still being tested and replicated outside the US. I also gave Friedman too little weight in my opening, where I proposed only Chetty and Hendren. His role in the tax-record data construction makes the three-name version more defensible. It is a strong alternative. I still see the conceptual originality of B027 as higher than the measurement contribution, and thirty years of replication versus roughly a decade is a real difference.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B027 third and puts B004 first. He argues that the political-economics credit is well concentrated in Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson, and that the 2024 prize recognised an adjacent but different strand.
responses.response: I agree that credit is well concentrated and that the 2024 prize is adjacent rather than identical. I would add that his own uncertainty list asks whether the empirical identification outweighs the theory. I do not think we should treat the 2024 prize as settled evidence of saturation either way. It should enter as a timing consideration, not a scientific one. I do not find B004 clearly stronger on novelty, because the 2022 prize overlaps substantially with that financial-frictions agenda.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give the 2024 institutions prize as a timing or novelty consideration for B027.
Whether the cross-country evidence on electoral rules and constitutions is credible enough, or whether later design-based work carries enough of the empirical case.
Whether the trio including Besley is better than the Persson-Tabellini pair. This turns on how the state-capacity strand is weighted against the constitutions-and-electoral-rules strand.
Whether B002 will mature enough to outrank B027 on common criteria, given continuing debate on the causal interpretation of place effects.
How to treat the other contributors in the wider political-economy field who are outside the credited names.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the credited names in B027. The profile lists no co-authorship with Persson, Tabellini or Besley. It records only an institutional overlap at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell), and these are fellow committee members rather than candidates. My co-authors (Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom, Oosterbeek, van Ours) are not credited on any shortlisted entry. My own field is empirical labour economics, so I may favour design-based evidence when assessing B002 and B024. This is a disclosure only and not a recusal.
